question: O que são os palácios espirituais?
expected:
- Identifica o termo hebraico 'heichalot' (היכלות, palácios/salões) como um conceito central da mística judaica: são câmaras ou níveis do mundo espiritual pelos quais se ascende em direção à Presença Divina.
- Explica a literatura de Heichalot e Merkavá (ex.: Heichalot Rabbati, Heichalot Zutarti), dos períodos talmúdico e pós-talmúdico: descreve a ascensão da alma do místico ('yored merkavá') através de sete palácios celestiais, guardados por anjos, até o Trono da Glória. Liga isso ao Ma'asé Merkavá (Ezequiel 1) e às restrições da Mishná sobre seu estudo.
- Explica os heichalot no Zohar: há seções inteiras (em Bereshit e em Pekudei) sobre os sete palácios da santidade, pelos quais as orações ascendem e são recebidas e elevadas. Paralelamente, há sete palácios da impureza (sitra achra). O Zohar também descreve os palácios do Gan Eden onde residem as almas dos justos.
- Explica o sentido conceitual na Cabala posterior (Cordovero e Ari): os palácios são 'recipientes' ou moradas que vestem as sefirot e a luz divina. Os sete heichalot são associados ao mundo de Beriá e correspondem às sefirot, servindo como intermediários entre a luz e os níveis inferiores.
- Menciona o uso chassídico: por exemplo, a parábola do Baal Shem Tov sobre o rei no palácio cercado de muralhas e ilusões, que são removidas por quem busca o rei com sinceridade. Também o ensinamento de que a oração e o serviço interior conduzem a alma pelos 'palácios'.
- Ressalta que a linguagem de palácios é metafórica e não espacial ou física. Descreve graus de revelação e de proximidade com D'us.

question: Shalom mon ami d'étude. Arrêtons-nous, sur l'histoire de Moshé ,quand il fait paître les brebis deYitro au dela du désert. Que sont ces brebis (petit bétail) et pourquoi ces brebis sont à Yitro ? Quel est le SOD, de cette histoire ? Que represente chaque élément (brebis,Yitro,Moshé,le désert,au-dea du desert) ? Donne des réponses et commentaires (si tu en as) au niveau du SOD et sois précis. Ecarte le sens simple (pshat). Merci pour ton aide précieuse.
expected:
- Situe le verset (Chemot 3:1 : « וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתְנוֹ כֹּהֵן מִדְיָן וַיִּנְהַג אֶת הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר וַיָּבֹא אֶל הַר הָאֱלֹהִים חֹרֵבָה ») et répond en français, en se concentrant sur le remez, le drach et le sod plutôt que sur le pchat.
- Les brebis (tson) représentent les âmes d'Israël (cf. Ézéchiel 34:31 « vous êtes Mes brebis… vous êtes des hommes »). Le Midrash présente la conduite du troupeau comme la préparation de Moshé à diriger Israël : l'épisode du chevreau et le verdict « tu feras paître Mon troupeau Israël ». Moshé est le Ra'aya Méhemna, le « berger fidèle » qui nourrit les âmes de émouna et de da'at.
- Yitro, prêtre de Midyan, représente le monde extérieur et les kelipot, ou la « sagesse » idolâtre qui a tout essayé. Que les brebis lui appartiennent exprime l'idée kabbalistique d'étincelles saintes (nitsotsot) ou d'âmes captives dans le domaine de la kelipa. Moshé, en les faisant paître, opère leur birour (élévation et rectification). La conversion ultérieure de Yitro (Zohar, parachat Yitro) montre l'aboutissement de ce processus : quand le « autre côté » reconnaît Hachem, Son Nom est glorifié et le Don de la Torah peut avoir lieu.
- Le désert (midbar) est, dans le Zohar et la Kabbale, le lieu désolé et le domaine de la sitra a'hra (« serpents, brûleurs et scorpions »). « A'har hamidbar » se lit en sod comme le fait de conduire les âmes au-delà de ce domaine, ou de traverser la kelipa pour l'élever. La conclusion du verset, « il arriva à la montagne de D.ieu, 'Horev », indique que ce travail mène à la révélation du Sinaï et du buisson ardent. On peut aussi mentionner la lecture du pchat chez Rachi (s'éloigner du vol) comme base morale sur laquelle se greffe le sod.
- Peut mentionner la tradition du Arizal sur les racines d'âmes (Moshé lié à Hevel, Yitro aux étincelles de Kaïn, les Kénites), et le lien avec la réparation par Moshé. Cela doit être présenté comme une tradition kabbalistique, sans détails inventés.
- Distingue clairement ce qui est sourcé (Midrash, Zohar, Arizal, 'Hassidout) des interprétations symboliques personnelles, et reste prudent et précis dans les références.

question: Shalom chers amis d'étude. Dis-moi si, au niveau du sod, qui a présenté les dix paroles ? Ein Sof ou Métatron ?
expected:
- Les Dix Paroles ont été dites par Hachem Lui-même, jamais par un ange ni par Métatron. Le texte dit « Vayedaber Elokim » (Exode 20:1), et la Guemara enseigne que « Anokhi » et « Lo yihyé lekha » ont été entendus « mipi haGuevoura », de la bouche même du Tout-Puissant (Makkot 24a).
- Métatron n'est qu'un ange, Sar haPanim. Le Talmud met explicitement en garde contre le fait de le confondre avec Dieu : il ne faut ni se tromper à son sujet ni lui attribuer l'autorité divine (Sanhedrin 38b, sur Exode 23:21). L'erreur d'Elisha ben Abouya (« Akher »), qui vit Métatron et pensa à « deux pouvoirs », est l'exemple classique (Haguiga 15a). Attribuer le don de la Torah à Métatron relève de cette hérésie de « shtei reshouyot ».
- L'Ein Sof en tant que tel est au-delà de toute révélation et de tout nom. Selon la Kabbale, Il se révèle à travers les Sefirot. Le Zohar relie les Dix Paroles aux dix Sefirot, et « Anokhi » à un niveau très élevé de la divinité, Keter ou le Nom révélé dans Tiferet et Malkhout selon les passages.
- Le notarikon « ANoKhI = Ana Nafshi Ketavit Yehavit » (« Moi-même J'ai écrit et donné ») souligne que Dieu S'est investi Lui-même dans le don de la Torah (Shabbat 105a). La 'Hassidout, notamment Habad, explique que « Anokhi » désigne l'Essence même, « mi she'Anokhi », au-delà même des niveaux de lumière de l'Ein Sof qui se révèlent.
- Réponse nuancée : ce n'est ni « l'Ein Sof » sans médiation au sens d'une essence dévoilée, ni Métatron. C'est Hachem Lui-même, dont l'Essence était présente, qui S'est révélé et a parlé à travers les Sefirot. Les anges, eux, étaient présents au Sinaï mais n'étaient pas les locuteurs.

question: Pourquoi l'arbre de la vie s'appelle Yilan ?
expected:
- Expliquer que « Ilan » (אילן, parfois transcrit « Yilan ») est le mot hébreu et araméen pour « arbre », synonyme de « Etz ». Dans la Torah, on trouve « Etz HaChayim » (Genèse 2:9), alors que l'araméen biblique et le Zohar emploient « ilan / ilana » (par ex. « Ilana deHayei », l'Arbre de Vie).
- Préciser qu'en Kabbale, « Ilan » (pluriel « Ilanot ») désigne aussi le schéma des dix Sefirot disposées en forme d'arbre. Les Ilanot sont les rouleaux et diagrammes kabbalistiques qui représentent la structure des mondes et des Sefirot.
- Expliquer le symbolisme de l'arbre : racine unique en haut (l'Ein Sof / Keter), tronc et branches qui s'étendent, influx (shefa) qui descend comme la sève. On parle souvent d'un arbre inversé, dont les racines sont en haut, image présente dès le Sefer HaBahir.
- Mentionner, en le présentant comme une explication traditionnelle de type remez/guématria, que אילן vaut 91, soit la somme des Noms יהוה (26) et אדני (65). Cela évoque l'union de Tiferet/Zeir Anpin et de Malkhout.

- Signaler éventuellement que « yılan » en turc signifie « serpent ». Il n'y a aucun lien avec le terme hébreu, ce qui permet de lever une confusion possible du questionneur.
- Répondre en français.

question: Tell me more about Shahar as the Don or morning and a divine being
expected:
- Clarifies that 'Shahar' (שחר) is the Hebrew word for dawn/daybreak, and that in ancient Canaanite/Ugaritic mythology Shahar was a deity of dawn, paired with Shalim (dusk) in the Ugaritic text known as 'The Birth of the Gracious Gods' (KTU 1.23).
- Explains that in the Hebrew Bible shachar is not a god. Poetic personifications such as the 'wings of the dawn' (Psalms 139:9), the 'eyelids of the dawn' (Job 3:9, 41:10), and God commanding the dawn (Job 38:12) present the dawn as a creation under God's control. Scholars see this as demythologizing older imagery.
- Discusses Isaiah 14:12, 'Heilel ben Shachar' (shining one, son of the dawn), as a taunt against the king of Babylon. Notes that modern scholars connect it to a Canaanite myth of a star-god who tried to ascend, that the later Christian 'Lucifer' reading comes via the Vulgate, and that Jewish commentators read it as referring to the Babylonian king.
- Covers rabbinic material: the angel who wrestled Jacob asks to leave 'for the dawn has risen' (Genesis 32:27), explained in Chullin 91b as the angel needing to sing praise at dawn. 'Ayelet HaShachar' (Psalms 22:1) is applied to Esther (Yoma 29a) and to the gradual dawning of redemption (Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 1:1).
- Gives kabbalistic/Zohar perspectives: dawn/morning is associated with Chesed and Abraham, who instituted Shacharit (Berakhot 26b). In the Zohar, 'Ayelet HaShachar' is a symbol of the Shekhinah/Malkhut, and the transition from night (Din/Gevurah) to dawn is a time of divine mercy. These are symbolic emanations or attributes, not separate deities.
- Stresses that Jewish monotheism rejects any independent divine being called Shahar, so any 'divinity' language must be framed historically (Canaanite religion) or as metaphor and personification.

question: In the prayers of the 18 benedictions, there are references to praying to God as our father and as our mother. This must be a reference to Kaballah and father and mother is part of Adam Kadmmon

The Binah–Imma link draws on the rabbinic wordplay on 'ki im la-binah tikra' (Proverbs 2:3) in Berakhot 57a.

They are not described as components of Adam Kadmon itself.

question: Who was responsible for writing the Zohar and was it only one person
expected:
- Traditional view: the Zohar records the teachings of the Tanna Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai (Rashbi, 2nd century CE) and his circle (the chevraya, e.g., R. Elazar his son, R. Abba, who is described as the scribe recording the teachings); this is the view accepted by most traditional Kabbalists and Chassidic and Sephardic authorities.
- The Zohar first appeared and circulated in late 13th-century Castile through Rabbi Moshe de Leon, who claimed to be copying from an ancient manuscript.

question: What is the correspondence of the four directions and the matriarchs?

question: I accept the profound connections between the reproductive organs and the symbol of covenant with God and of the sefirah of Yesod (foundation). But others who have been circumcised, whether Jewish, Muslim or anyone else, are still perfectly capable of the most severe types of abusive actions using their reproductive organs, and this is actually common. - Tone: respectful toward the user's observation and toward other religions, while clearly presenting the Jewish view.

question: Peut tu me dire si les prophetes et tsadikim ont laissé des pistes sur l'essence divine ?
expected:
- The central teaching is that God's essence (Atsmout) cannot be grasped by any created being, not even a prophet. Moïse asked « Montre-moi Ta gloire » and was told « l'homme ne peut Me voir et vivre ». He was shown only « Mon dos » (Exode 33:18-23). Rambam explains this as knowledge of God through His effects, not His essence (Yessodé HaTorah 1:10).
- The prophets repeat that God is incomparable and unsearchable: « À qui Me comparerez-vous ? » (Isaïe 40:18, 25), « Mes pensées ne sont pas vos pensées » (Isaïe 55:8-9), « Sa grandeur est insondable » (Psaumes 145:3), and « Peux-tu atteindre le fond de Dieu ? » (Iyov 11:7).
- What can be known is God's actions and attributes of conduct (middot), not His essence. Examples are the 13 attributes of mercy (Exode 34:6-7) and Jérémie 9:23 (« connaître Moi… que Je suis l'Éternel qui fait la bonté, le droit et la justice »). Rambam reads these as attributes of action and develops negative theology: we can say only what God is not (Guide des égarés I:54, I:58).
- Prophetic visions such as Isaïe 6 and Ézéchiel 1 are carefully qualified (« l'apparence de la ressemblance de la gloire »). The Sages and Rambam treat them as images and parables, not depictions of the essence. Rambam stresses that God has no body (Yessodé HaTorah 1:7-9).
- The Kabbalistic and Hassidic tradition distinguishes the Ein Sof, which is beyond all thought (« leit mahchava tefissa bakh klal », Patah Éliyahou in the Tikounei Zohar), from the Sefirot through which God reveals Himself. Hassidut, for example the Tanya, also speaks of Atsmout.
- A good answer should end with a nuance. The « pistes » the tzaddikim left are mainly the path of knowing God through His works, the Torah and the commandments, and imitating His attributes (« comme Il est miséricordieux, sois miséricordieux »). They also teach that recognizing the limits of knowledge is itself a form of knowledge (« le but du savoir est de savoir qu'on ne sait pas », Bechinat Olam / Bahya).

question: Como melhorar os meus pensamento?
expected:
- Responder em português, com tom prático e encorajador, reconhecendo que a Torá dá grande importância aos pensamentos (ex.: 'hirhurei aveirá kashin me-aveirá' — os pensamentos de pecado são piores que o próprio pecado, Yoma 29a).
- Estratégia central da tradição judaica: ocupar a mente com Torá e pensamentos positivos — a mente não fica vazia, por isso substitui-se o mau pensamento por um bom (Rambam, Issurei Biá 21:19; Tanya cap. 12 sobre afastar o pensamento e não lutar diretamente com ele).
- Guardar os olhos e os sentidos: 'velo taturu acharei levavchem ve-acharei eineichem' (Números 15:39) — o que se vê e ouve molda o pensamento; escolher o ambiente e as influências.
- Hábitos de mussar: cheshbon hanefesh (autoavaliação diária), estudo regular de livros de mussar (Mesilat Yesharim, Chovot HaLevavot, Tanya), e repetição/meditação de ideias positivas.
- A ação influencia o coração: 'acharei hapeulot nimshachim halevavot' (Sefer HaChinuch, mitzvá 16) — boas ações e rotinas mudam gradualmente o pensamento.
- Atitude perante pensamentos indesejados: não desesperar nem sentir culpa excessiva por pensamentos involuntários; o mérito está em afastá-los (Tanya cap. 27); cultivar bitachon, gratidão e olhar favorável sobre os outros (lekaf zechut).
- Oração e pedido de ajuda divina (ex.: 'veha'er eineinu betoratecha', 'lev tahor bera li Elokim' — Salmos 51:12); e, se os pensamentos forem obsessivos ou angustiantes, procurar orientação de um rabino e/ou profissional de saúde mental.

question: Soy No Judio, quiero acercarme a Dios, existe un Siddur en Español? me puedes dar una guia para empezar desde cero a acercarme a Dios?
expected:
- Responder en español, con un tono cálido y respetuoso. Afirmar que, según el judaísmo, un no judío puede y es bienvenido a acercarse a Dios y a rezarle directamente. Por ejemplo, Isaías 56:7 habla de una «casa de oración para todos los pueblos», y en la plegaria de Salomón (1 Reyes 8:41-43) se ruega por el extranjero que viene a orar. No hace falta convertirse para tener una relación con Dios.
- Explicar el marco de las Siete Leyes de los Hijos de Noé (Sanhedrín 56a; Rambam, Hiljot Melajim 9:1). Quien las observa por reconocerlas como mandato divino es considerado de los «piadosos de las naciones» y tiene parte en el Mundo Venidero (Rambam, Melajim 8:11). Este es el punto de partida.
- Confirmar que existen sidurim con traducción al español y que se consiguen en librerías judías y editoriales. Aclarar que el sidur fue redactado para judíos: frases como «que nos santificó con Sus mandamientos y nos ordenó» o «que nos eligió» no se ajustan a un no judío. Conviene adaptarlas u omitirlas, o usar materiales de oración pensados para Bnei Noaj.
- Guía práctica para empezar: oración personal y espontánea en su propio idioma, que es plenamente válida; lectura de Tehilim (Salmos); estudio de las leyes noájidas y de la Torá relevante para ellas; gratitud diaria, por ejemplo agradecer al despertar o antes y después de comer; y conducta ética.
- Señalar los límites: un no judío no debe inventar una religión nueva ni asumir como obligación los preceptos específicos de Israel, como guardar Shabat plenamente o ponerse tefilín (Rambam, Melajim 10:9). Sí puede dar caridad, rezar y hacer el bien.
- Recomendar buscar orientación de un rabino ortodoxo o de organizaciones noájidas reconocidas. Mencionar que el judaísmo no busca convertir a nadie, pero que la conversión existe si la persona lo desea en el futuro.

question: Почему изучение талмуда вавилонского положительно влияет на чистоту мыслей и на мыслительный процесс у человека в положительную сторону
expected:
- Чистота мыслей: Тора названа противоядием (тавлин) против йецер ха-ра — «Я сотворил злое начало и сотворил Тору как приправу/противоядие» (Кидушин 30б); «если встретил тебя этот мерзкий — тащи его в бейт-мидраш». Рамбам (Иссурей Биа 22:21) пишет, что мысли о запретном возникают лишь в сердце, свободном от мудрости, и советует направлять ум к словам Торы.
- Святость самого изучения: Тора — слово Б-га, её изучение соединяет разум человека с Б-жественной мудростью и освящает мысль (Тания гл. 5 о единении знающего с познаваемым). Также Нефеш ха-Хаим (ч. 4) о Торе как источнике святости.
- Развитие мышления: Вавилонский Талмуд построен как диалектика (шакля ве-тария) — вопросы, ответы, опровержения, сравнения, логические выводы (каль ва-хомер и др.), что тренирует точность, критичность, способность видеть разные стороны и отличать тонкие различия.
- Талмуд Бавли назван «темным» (Санхедрин 24а: «במחשכים הושיבני — זה תלמוד בבלי»), т.е. требует глубокой работы ума; именно поэтому он является основным предметом углублённого изучения в ешивах.
- Тора лишма и ее влияние на характер: изучение ради Небес облачает человека в смирение и трепет (Пиркей Авот 6:1); но знание без страха Небес и мусара не гарантирует чистоты — нужна правильная цель и сочетание с работой над качествами.
- Ответ на русском, сбалансированно: различать традиционные духовные объяснения и интеллектуальные/психологические, не делать необоснованных «научных» утверждений.

question: Shalom ! Quand la Torah ne parle pas d'un sujet est ce cela signifie qu'il l'autorise ?
expected:
- Répondre en français. Préciser que « Torah » inclut la Torah écrite et la Torah orale (Talmud, Midrash, poskim) : beaucoup de sujets absents du texte écrit sont traités par la tradition orale et les décisionnaires. L'absence dans le verset ne signifie donc pas l'absence de position de la Torah.
- Les Sages ont autorité pour légiférer et étendre la loi (lo tassour, Deutéronome 17:11 ; décrets et enactments rabbiniques). Les questions nouvelles (technologie, médecine…) sont tranchées par analogie et par principes, pas automatiquement permises.
- Le Ramban (Lévitique 19:2, « Kedochim tihyou ») enseigne qu'on peut être un « naval birchout haTorah », un être vil en restant dans les limites de la loi, et que la Torah donne un commandement général de sainteté et de modération. Le silence explicite ne vaut donc pas approbation morale.
- Le Ramban sur Deutéronome 6:18 (« Tu feras ce qui est droit et bon ») explique que la Torah ne peut détailler chaque situation et donne un principe général de droiture et de lifnim mi-chourat hadin.
- Le Talmud montre que certaines valeurs découlent de la raison et du derekh erets indépendamment d'un verset explicite. Par exemple, Yoma 67b : les michpatim « auraient mérité d'être écrits ». Erouvin 100b : on aurait appris la pudeur du chat.

question: Unidad de Dios, Panteismo, Israel, Dios para la creacion?
expected:
- La unidad de Dios (Shemá, Deut. 6:4) es el fundamento de la fe judía. Según Rambam no es una unidad numérica ni compuesta, sino absolutamente simple e incomparable. Dios es incorpóreo y no depende de nada.
- El panteísmo clásico (p. ej. Spinoza: Dios = naturaleza) es rechazado por el judaísmo tradicional: Dios es Creador trascendente, anterior al mundo e independiente de él; el mundo no es Dios.
- La Cabalá y el Jasidut afirman además que nada existe fuera de Dios ('ein od milvadó', Deut. 4:35, 39). Dios llena y rodea todos los mundos ('memalé / sovev kol almin'), según el Zohar y el Tania, Shaar HaYijud VehaEmuná. Esta postura suele describirse como panenteísmo o acosmismo, no como panteísmo. Debe distinguirse con claridad de la identificación de Dios con el mundo.
- Israel tiene el papel de testigo y portador de la unidad divina en el mundo ('Vosotros sois Mis testigos', Is. 43:10). Según Berajot 6a, Dios e Israel se proclaman mutuamente 'únicos'. La elección de Israel es una misión, no una superioridad racial.
- Propósito de la creación: Dios no necesita nada y crea por pura bondad, para beneficiar a otros (Ramjal, Derej Hashem). Otras fuentes señalan Su gloria (Is. 43:7; Avot 6:11). El Midrash habla de 'una morada en los mundos inferiores' (Tanjumá Nasó 16; Tania cap. 36). Una idea relacionada es que el mundo fue creado por la Torá y por Israel (Rashi sobre Gen. 1:1).
- Una buena respuesta presenta varias corrientes (filosófica/Rambam frente a cabalística/jasídica) sin fusionarlas, y responde en español.

question: E tenho milhões de perguntas durante toda minha vida, eu sou cristão, e percebi que o espiritismo se identifica muito com o judaísmo em algumas, como a não existência do inferno e sim uma espécie de purgatório de purificação, e reencarnação etc
expected:
- Responder em português, com respeito, tratando a observação implícita (o espiritismo e o judaísmo são parecidos?) e mostrando semelhanças e diferenças reais.
- Guehinom: no judaísmo rabínico é sobretudo um processo de purificação temporário. Para a maioria, dura no máximo doze meses (Mishná Eduyot 2:10; Rosh Hashaná 17a). Isso se parece com a ideia de purgatório. Mas há categorias de pecadores graves para quem a Guemará fala de punição duradoura. Não é correto dizer que o judaísmo nega toda punição eterna.
- Reencarnação (guilgul neshamot): não aparece explicitamente na Bíblia nem no Talmud. Rav Saadia Gaon a rejeitou (Emunot veDeot). Foi amplamente aceita na Cabalá (Zohar; Arizal, Sha'ar HaGilgulim) e por vários comentaristas, como o Ramban (em Jó). Hoje é a visão predominante em grande parte do mundo ortodoxo. Seu propósito é o tikun (correção) de missões ou mitsvot não cumpridas, e não uma evolução espiritual universal e obrigatória como no espiritismo kardecista.
- Diferença central: a Torá proíbe explicitamente consultar os mortos, médiuns e necromantes (Deuteronômio 18:10-12; Levítico 19:31, 20:6, 20:27; o caso de Saul e a necromante de En-Dor). A prática mediúnica, que é o núcleo do espiritismo, é portanto proibida pelo judaísmo.
- Outras diferenças: o judaísmo é centrado na Torá, nas mitsvot e na relação de aliança com D'us. question: Qual a recompensa de um escriba na era messiânica e no olam haba ?
expected:
- A resposta deve ser em português. Deve dizer com honestidade que não há uma fonte clássica que descreva uma recompensa específica e distinta para o sofer STaM na era messiânica, em contraste com o olam haba. A resposta deve se apoiar nos princípios gerais e evitar promessas detalhadas inventadas.
- O trabalho do escriba é chamado de 'trabalho celestial' (melechet shamayim). Rabi Yishmael advertiu Rabi Meir que omitir ou acrescentar uma letra pode 'destruir o mundo' (Eruvin 13a). Os escribas de livros, tefilin e mezuzot estão todos ocupados com trabalho celestial (Pesachim 50b). A mesma passagem nota que quem faz isso visando lucro não vê sinal de bênção, ou seja, a intenção conta.
- Sobre o valor da escrita do Sefer Torá, Menachot 30a ensina: quem escreve um Sefer Torá é como se o tivesse recebido no Sinai, e quem corrige uma só letra é como se o tivesse escrito inteiro. O escriba também possibilita as mitsvot de muitos (tefilin, mezuzá, leitura da Torá), com o mérito de zikui harabim.
- A recompensa essencial das mitsvot não é paga neste mundo (Kidushin 39b; 'sechar mitsvá behai alma leca'). Não se conhece a medida da recompensa de cada mitsvá (Avot 2:1).
- A resposta deve distinguir os conceitos. Para o Rambam, a era messiânica ocorre neste mundo, sem mudança na ordem natural, e visa permitir o estudo da Torá e as mitsvot sem opressão (Hilchot Melachim 12). O olam haba é a recompensa espiritual da alma, cujo bem não pode ser descrito (Hilchot Teshuvá 8). Outros, como Ramban/Shaar HaGemul, veem o olam haba após a ressurreição.
- Pode mencionar que 'sofrim' também designa os sábios desde Ezra, o Escriba. Pode mencionar Daniel 12:3 ('os sábios brilharão... como as estrelas'), aplicado em Bava Batra 8b aos que ensinam/justificam o povo. Essas aplicações são gerais e não específicas ao sofer STaM.

question: Quando a pessoa pode e Quando a pessoa não pode se converter?
expected:
- Judaism does not actively seek converts, but sincere conversion (giyur) is accepted; the Talmud describes initially discouraging the candidate and informing him of some commandments and of the hardships of Jewish life (Yevamot 47a-b).
- The essential requirement is sincere acceptance of the commandments (kabbalat ol mitzvot). Without it the conversion is not valid according to mainstream halacha.
- The process requires a beit din of three, circumcision for men (or hatafat dam brit if already circumcised) and immersion in a mikveh for men and women.
- Conversion for ulterior motives (marriage, money, status, fear) is not accepted l'chatchila. Yevamot 24b and the Rambam note that converts were not accepted in the days of David and Solomon. Post facto (b'dieved) such converts are considered converts (Rambam Issurei Biah 13:17). Some later authorities permitted conversion in marriage cases when the candidate is sincere.
- Who cannot convert or faces restrictions: a minor converts only through a beit din, with the right to protest on reaching majority (Ketubot 11a). Someone lacking mental capacity cannot make a valid acceptance of mitzvot. Someone already Jewish by maternal lineage does not need conversion.
- A good answer should explain that the decision rests with a recognized beit din, that standards vary between institutions, and should advise contacting a rabbi or recognized conversion program.
- A Noahide path (the 7 Noahide laws) is a valid alternative for non-Jews who do not wish to take on all the mitzvot.

question: Um não judeu que doa para yeshivot e projetos de kiruv tem méritos?
expected:
- Sim: um não judeu que apoia o estudo da Torá e boas causas recebe recompensa; o princípio talmúdico é que 'o Santo, bendito seja, não priva de recompensa nenhuma criatura' (אין הקב"ה מקפח שכר כל בריה).
- Os não judeus (Bnei Noach) são obrigados às sete leis de Noé, mas podem fazer atos de bondade e caridade adicionais e receber mérito por eles. O Rambam diz que os justos das nações que observam as sete leis por serem ordenadas por Deus têm parte no Mundo Vindouro.
- A halachá permite aceitar doações de não judeus para fins de caridade e instituições, com algumas ressalvas. O Talmud traz o caso de Ifra Hormiz, mãe do rei Shapur, cuja doação foi aceita.
- O Talmud (Bava Batra 10b) discute a caridade das nações à luz de Provérbios 14:34, dizendo que às vezes ela é feita por vaidade ou autopromoção. Isso ressalta que a intenção sincera, em reconhecimento a Deus, aumenta o valor do ato, sem anular o mérito.
- Há exemplos históricos de não judeus que apoiaram a Torá e Israel e foram louvados, como Antonino, amigo de Rabi Yehudá HaNassi. Também há a visão dos profetas sobre estrangeiros que se ligam ao Deus de Israel (Isaías 56).
- A resposta deve deixar claro que não é necessário converter-se para ter mérito. Ao mesmo tempo, deve distinguir o mérito do não judeu das obrigações e parcerias específicas de judeus, como o modelo Issachar-Zevulun, sem exagerar nem minimizar.

question: Um gentio que não é idolatra e segue as sete leis de noach e doas para o estudo de torah ele tem um mérito semelhante ao de um yehudi?
expected:
- The answer must affirm that a gentile who keeps the seven Noahide laws has great value and merit. Per Rambam (Melachim 8:11), if he accepts them as commanded by God through Moshe Rabbeinu, he is among the chasidei umot ha-olam and has a share in the World to Come.
- It must cite Rabbi Meir's statement (Sanhedrin 59a; Bava Kamma 38a): a gentile who studies Torah is like a Kohen Gadol. The Gemara explains this refers to study connected to his own seven mitzvot. This shows the high standing a righteous gentile can reach.
- It must say that supporting Torah study and giving tzedakah are real merits for a gentile too. The answer can mention the Yissachar–Zevulun model (whoever supports Torah shares in its merit) as an analogy. Gentiles' donations and offerings were also accepted in the Temple.
- It must explain the difference from a Jew. A Jew is obligated in 613 mitzvot, and 'greater is one who is commanded and does than one who is not commanded and does' (Kiddushin 31a). So the merit is not identical in kind, since the gentile acts as a non-obligated person. Still, God rewards everyone fully according to his role and deeds.
- Ideally, the answer notes the tradition that, by the standard of deeds, anyone can reach spiritual heights. Tanna Devei Eliyahu says that, whether Jew or gentile, according to one's deeds the holy spirit rests on him.
- It should answer in Portuguese, in a respectful and encouraging tone, without diminishing the Noahide.

question: Perhaps as part of our religion in Judaism, as in other God wishes us to witness, envision the destruction of creation in order to better achieve the world to come and a cheap balance in this world. This would not seem to be for everyone, even those who are religious. This vision is available through the writings of prophecy and also the fall of Zion is described by Rabbi Luotto in the book on redemption in order to teach and face a dreadful possibilities in this world in a positive light.
expected:
- Should briefly clarify the somewhat unclear question, and should reasonably identify 'Rabbi Luotto' as probably Ramchal (R. Moshe Chaim Luzzatto) and his Ma'amar HaGeulah. It should flag this as a likely identification, not a certainty.
- Should explain that Judaism does not ask people to imagine the destruction of creation as a spiritual exercise for its own sake. Prophetic and rabbinic descriptions of destruction (the Churban, chevlei Mashiach, the 'desolate' millennium) always point toward repair, teshuvah and redemption, never toward despair or world-negation.
- Should present the legitimate related practices. Mourning for Jerusalem is one: Tisha B'Av, Tikkun Chatzot, and the teaching 'whoever mourns Jerusalem merits to see its joy'. Recalling the day of death as a tool against the yetzer hara is another (Berakhot 5a). Both serve this-worldly avodah and appreciation of life.
- Should note R. Akiva's model in Makkot 24b. He laughed at seeing foxes on the ruined Temple Mount, because the fulfillment of the prophecies of destruction guarantees the prophecies of consolation. This is the classic way of facing dreadful realities 'in a positive light'.
- Should note the rabbinic ambivalence about the birthpangs of Mashiach. Some Amoraim said 'let him come, but may I not see him' (Sanhedrin 98b). Rambam warns against dwelling on eschatological details and calculating the end (Hilchot Melachim 12:2). Apocalyptic fixation is therefore discouraged.
- Should affirm that this world has real value in Judaism. It is the place of mitzvot and tikkun, and the World to Come is earned through living rightly in it, not through contemplating its end. Balance and simcha are emphasized, for example in Mesillat Yesharim and Ramchal's broader system.
- Should agree that intense contemplation of destruction is not suitable for everyone. It can lead to despair, so it should be approached with guidance and balance.

question: The book of Job refers to the Sabens steal away the animals. question: Yes, I want to start off with a dvar Torah on all of Freud's chiddushim, but bring them out through the Torah and show how all these psychological concepts are in the Torah.

question: In slavery aren't all of these perspectives in tension but perhaps productively. Hashem is absolutely moral (this is what belief in one G-d means) but how does a unitary infinite interact with the physical world of man? There is no a priori map for that and it needs perforce to be in tension between divine and man. Why not abolish slavery in the torah? We don't know but like Abraham we need to ask but asking isnt the same as making ourselves G-d.
expected:
- Engages the user's framing directly: affirms that the Torah's treatment of slavery involves real tension between absolute divine morality and a Torah given to human beings in a particular historical-social reality. It does not dismiss the question or offer facile apologetics.
- Presents the classic gradualist/accommodation approach: Rambam (Guide III:32) explains that the Torah does not uproot entrenched human practices all at once (his example is sacrifices). Many later thinkers apply this to slavery. Make clear that the application to slavery is an extension, not Rambam's explicit example.
- Shows how the Torah radically regulates and humanizes the institution. Eved ivri: release in the seventh year (Exodus 21:2) and the ear-piercing rebuke (Kiddushin 22b). Freedom for loss of a tooth or eye (Exodus 21:26-27). Punishment for killing a slave (Exodus 21:20). The ban on returning an escaped slave (Deuteronomy 23:16-17). The Sabbath rest for slaves rooted in the memory of Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:14-15). Kiddushin 20a: one who acquires a Hebrew servant 'acquires a master for himself.'
- Distinguishes eved ivri from eved kenaani and honestly acknowledges the harsher laws for the latter (e.g., Leviticus 25:46). Also notes Rambam (Hilkhot Avadim 9:8): the law permits harsh work, but the way of piety and wisdom is to be merciful. He grounds this in the shared humanity of master and slave (citing Job 31:15).
- Affirms the legitimacy of questioning within faith: Abraham's 'Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justice?' (Genesis 18:25), and also Moshe and Jeremiah. Balances this with humility before divine wisdom (e.g., Job 38). This agrees with the user's point that asking is not the same as making oneself God.
- Notes that the Torah's own values (the Exodus narrative, human dignity as tzelem Elokim) arguably contain the seeds of the institution's eventual obsolescence. It also notes that Jewish practice of slavery effectively lapsed historically.
- Presents these as a range of perspectives that can coexist, not a single definitive answer.

question: Would the Torah approve of AI?
expected:
- The Torah has no explicit statement about AI, so any answer comes from applying general principles. Technology is generally viewed as morally neutral: its value depends on how it is used. Human creativity and mastery of the world are part of the mandate to 'fill the earth and subdue it' (Gen. 1:28) and to be partners in creation.
- Precedents for artificial beings: the golem traditions in Sanhedrin 65b (Rava creates a man, R. Zeira says 'return to your dust'; it could not speak). Later discussions include Chakham Tzvi on whether a golem counts for a minyan. These show the tradition entertained human-made 'intelligence' without banning it, while distinguishing it from a human with a soul.
- Key distinction: humans are created b'tzelem Elokim (in God's image) and have nishmat chayim (the breath of life) and moral free will (bechira). AI lacks a soul, moral agency and halachic personhood, so it cannot replace human moral responsibility.
- Concerns the Torah would raise: idolatry-like over-reliance or deification of human-made creations, as in the Rambam's account of how idolatry began; deception (geneivat da'at) and falsehood; privacy and lashon hara; harm; and the moral responsibility of the creators and users.
- In Torah study and psak, AI may serve as a tool, but halachic decisions require human judgment, mesorah and a qualified posek. Torah is 'not in heaven' (lo bashamayim hi), so authority rests with human sages.
- A balanced conclusion: the Torah neither blanketly approves nor condemns AI. It is permitted and potentially valuable when used ethically and in the service of good, with appropriate caution.

question: When the Rambam says Hashem can't destroy or duplicate himself, isn't that limiting G-d?
expected:
- Identifies the source: in Moreh Nevuchim (Guide III:15) the Rambam says the impossible has a fixed nature that is not 'made', and that God cannot bring into being another like Himself, annihilate Himself, become corporeal, or change; he gives logical examples like a square whose diagonal equals its side.
- Core answer: for the Rambam, omnipotence means power over everything possible. A logical contradiction is not a 'thing' that God fails to do. It is a meaningless combination of words, so failing to 'do' it is no deficiency or limitation.
- Duplication: God is by definition the one uncaused, necessarily existent, absolutely simple Being (Yesodei HaTorah 1:1-7). Anything God 'made' would be caused and created, and so by definition not another God. 'A second God' is a self-contradiction, and God's uniqueness is itself a perfection.
- Self-destruction: God's existence is necessary (Yesodei HaTorah 1:1-3). Being subject to destruction or change would be a deficiency, so being unable to cease existing is a mark of perfection, not a weakness.
- Connects this to the Rambam's negative theology (Guide I:50-60). Saying God 'cannot' perish or be multiplied really denies imperfection of Him; it does not impose a limit on Him.
- Notes, briefly and fairly, that some later thinkers, especially in kabbalistic and Chassidic thought, express a different emphasis: God as beyond logical categories, e.g., the idea that God is 'nimna ha-nimna'ot', able to hold opposites. This is presented as an alternative view, while the Rambam's position remains the classic rationalist answer.

question: Explicame mas, explicame todo sobre Sucot
expected:

It also covers the structure of Yom Tov days versus Chol HaMoed.
- The mitzvah of the sukkah: one dwells in the sukkah for seven days in memory of the clouds of glory or the huts in the desert, the dispute of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Akiva in Sukkah 11b (Leviticus 23:42-43). question: Just give me what year we are in for maaser and teruma for growing produce in the land of Israel with the appropriate brachot to say this year and a very short short instruction on the coin and amount to remove
expected:
- Identify the year in the shmita cycle. 5782 was shmita. 5785 is year 3, so maaser ani applies. 5786 (from Rosh Hashana, Sept. 2025) is year 4, so maaser sheni applies. 5787 is year 5 (maaser sheni), 5788 is year 6 (maaser ani), and 5789 is the next shmita.
- The answer should name the Hebrew year it assumes, or give both 5785 and 5786.
- Explain briefly which year's rules apply to a given crop. For tree fruit it depends on when the fruit budded (chanata), with Tu BiShvat as the new year for trees. For vegetables it depends on when they were picked. For grains and legumes it depends on when they reached one-third of their growth. Produce from a year-3 budding may still need maaser ani even after Rosh Hashana.
- State the order and amounts. First remove slightly more than 1% for terumah gedolah and terumat maaser together. Then designate maaser rishon (10%). Then designate maaser sheni or maaser ani, depending on the year (10% of the remainder). Only the slightly-more-than-1% piece is physically removed.
- The removed piece is wrapped (often double-wrapped) and disposed of respectfully. It may not be eaten.
- Recite the declaration (nusach) for designating the portions.

- Coin: in a maaser sheni year, redeem the maaser sheni onto a designated coin worth at least a pruta. Common practice is to use a 'perutah chamurah' coin or a share in a coin fund (e.g., Machon HaTorah VeHaAretz), redeeming onto a pruta's worth. When the coin fills up, it is destroyed or disposed of and not used.
- In a maaser ani year there is no redemption and no coin. For definitely tevel produce, maaser ani belongs to the poor.
- Mention biur maaserot on erev Pesach and vidui maaser at the end of Pesach in year 4 (5786). Advise consulting a rabbi or a guide such as Machon HaTorah VeHaAretz.

question: If a child is born in Adar I, and when he turns 13 there are two Adars, will the bar mitzvah be in Adar I or Adar II?
expected:
- The child was born in Adar I, so his birth year was a leap year. If the year he turns 13 is also a leap year, he becomes bar mitzvah on the same date in Adar I, the month he was actually born in. This is the accepted ruling (Rema, OC 55:10; Mishnah Berurah there).
- This differs from a child born in Adar of an ordinary year who turns 13 in a leap year. For him the Rema rules that the bar mitzvah is in Adar II. Some authorities disagree, and the answer may mention that this is debated.
- Do not confuse this case with yahrzeit or other Adar issues, where different considerations apply (e.g., OC 568:7). For a bar mitzvah, a child born in Adar I or Adar II keeps his own Adar when the 13th year is also a leap year.
- Halachic adulthood (obligation in mitzvot, counting for a minyan) begins at nightfall at the start of his birthday date. The celebration or aliyah can be scheduled accordingly.
- Because calendar details can be tricky, a good answer recommends confirming the exact date with a rabbi.

Do not confuse this case with yahrzeit or other Adar issues, where different considerations apply (e.g., OC 568:7). For a bar mitzvah, a child born in Adar I or Adar II keeps his own Adar when the 13th year is also a leap year.
Halachic adulthood (obligation in mitzvot, counting for a minyan) begins at nightfall at the start of his birthday date. The celebration or aliyah can be scheduled accordingly.
Because calendar details can be tricky, a good answer recommends confirming the exact date with a rabbi.
rubric.community_notes: For a child born in Adar I whose 13th year is a leap year, there is broad consensus across communities that the bar mitzvah is in Adar I. Differences between communities and authorities arise mainly in the related case of a child born in a non-leap year who turns 13 in a leap year. The Rema, followed by Ashkenazim, rules Adar II; some authorities dispute this.
pitfalls: Saying the bar mitzvah is in Adar II by misapplying the rule for a child born in an ordinary year
Saying it is always Adar II, or that the family may choose freely
Confusing the bar mitzvah rule with the yahrzeit rule
Inventing sources or misattributing the Rema's ruling to the Mechaber
Not noting that the bar mitzvah takes effect from nightfall

question: Until what time at night may one recite the evening Shema?
expected:
- The Mishnah (Berakhot 1:1) records a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says until the end of the first watch; the Sages say until midnight; Rabban Gamliel says until dawn (alot ha-shachar).
- The Sages' midnight limit is a rabbinic safeguard (seyag) to keep people from delaying and missing the mitzvah. Biblically, the time extends until dawn.
- Halacha (Rambam; Shulchan Arukh OC 235:3): the ideal is to recite before midnight (chatzot). If one delayed, whether deliberately or not, one may still recite with its blessings until alot ha-shachar.
- After dawn and before sunrise, one fulfills the obligation only under duress (ones), such as being drunk, ill or otherwise prevented (SA OC 235:4; Berakhot 8b). Even then, Hashkiveinu is omitted, and there are details about the blessings.
- Halachic midnight is not 12:00 on the clock. It is commonly computed as the midpoint between sunset and sunrise (equivalently, 12 seasonal hours after midday), so it varies by location and season. One should check a local zmanim calendar.
- Practical advice: recite promptly after nightfall (tzeit). Bedtime Shema does not replace the Maariv obligation if it is said after the deadline. Consult a rabbi for specific situations.

question: Why do we make birchas hachama every 28 years when precise tekufah measurements do not correspond with the 28 year cycle?
expected:
- The source is Berakhot 59b (baraita): one who sees the sun 'bitkufatah' blesses 'Oseh ma'aseh bereishit', which Abaye explains as every 28 years, when the tekufah of Nisan falls in Saturn on Tuesday night going into Wednesday. Codified in Rambam, Hilchot Berakhot 10:18 and Shulchan Arukh OC 229:2.
- The 28-year cycle comes from Shmuel's model (tekufat Shmuel), which uses a 365¼-day solar year (52 weeks + 1¼ days). After 28 years (4×7), the tekufah returns to the same hour and weekday. This is effectively the Julian year, which is why the blessing now falls around April 8 rather than at the true March equinox.
- Chazal and the Rishonim knew this was an approximation. Rav Ada bar Ahava's figure is more accurate (Rambam, Kiddush HaChodesh 9–10). Rambam explicitly calls Shmuel's tekufah an approximation, and the true astronomical equinox drifts relative to it by about 1 day per ~128 years.
- The answer should explain why the approximate cycle is kept anyway. The blessing commemorates the sun's position at Creation, when the luminaries were made on the fourth day; it is a halachic or commemorative cycle defined by Chazal rather than an astronomical observation. Halacha also adopted tekufat Shmuel as the operative convention in other contexts, such as starting the request for rain (tal umatar) in the Diaspora 60 days after the tekufah.
- Many Acharonim discussed the discrepancy and defended or explained the practice. Their explanations include: a fixed, uniform cycle is needed so the mitzvah does not depend on individual calculation; the blessing is on the 'cycle', not the exact equinox; and Chazal established the takkanah per Shmuel. Some noted the theoretical difficulty without changing practice.
- The answer should acknowledge honestly that the date does not match the real equinox. Universal practice nevertheless follows the Talmudic 28-year cycle (recent occurrences 1981 and 2009, next in 2037), recited in the morning of the Wednesday.

question: What is the significance of the 17th of Tammuz?
expected:
- Five calamities occurred on 17 Tammuz according to Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6: the Tablets were broken (Moses descending Sinai), the daily Tamid offering ceased (during the First Temple siege per tradition), the walls of Jerusalem were breached (Second Temple), Apostomus burned a Torah scroll, and an idol was placed in the Sanctuary (Heikhal).
- Note the Talmudic discussion (Ta'anit 28b; Jerusalem Talmud) that in the First Temple period the walls were breached on 9 Tammuz (Jeremiah 39:2), while the fast commemorates the Second Temple breach on the 17th.
- It is one of the four fasts mentioned in Zechariah 8:19 ('the fast of the fourth month'), a minor public fast from dawn to nightfall. Its observance includes Selichot, the Torah reading of Vayechal, and Aneinu.
- It begins the Three Weeks (bein ha-metzarim), the mourning period culminating in Tisha B'Av, with associated mourning customs.
- Theme: repentance and mourning for the Temple's destruction, with the hope that the fast will become a day of joy (Zechariah 8:19).

pitfalls: Claiming the First Temple walls were breached on the 17th without noting Jeremiah 39:2 and the 9th of Tammuz.

Failing to mention that it starts the Three Weeks.

question: What are the misur and trumah blessings for the year 5786
expected:
- Interprets 'misur and trumah' as the separation of terumot and ma'asrot (tithes) on Land of Israel produce, and explains the blessing and declaration recited when separating them.
- The blessing, said only on produce that is certainly untithed (tevel vadai), is: 'Barukh atah... asher kideshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu lehafrish terumot u-ma'asrot.' No blessing is said on demai (doubtfully tithed) produce.
- 5786 is the 4th year of the shemitah cycle (5782 was shemitah). The second tithe is therefore ma'aser sheni, not ma'aser ani (ma'aser ani applies only in years 3 and 6). The declaration should name ma'aser sheni and its redemption on a coin.
- Outlines the standard declaration: terumah gedolah, ma'aser rishon, terumat ma'aser (1/100), then ma'aser sheni redeemed onto a designated coin (at least a perutah, or using a peruta chamura).
- The year of produce is determined by its own rules, not simply the calendar date. Vegetables go by harvest date relative to Rosh Hashanah. Tree fruit goes by chanatah (budding/fruit formation) relative to Tu BiShvat. So some fruit eaten in 5786 may still be 3rd-year (5785) ma'aser ani produce.
- Notes that erev Pesach 5786 (spring 2026) is the time of biur ma'asrot (removal of tithes) for the 4th year of the cycle. Vidui ma'aser is recited on the last day of Pesach, customarily at Mincha, without a blessing.
- Advises using a reliable printed nusach (e.g., from the Chief Rabbinate or a kashrut/agricultural institute) and consulting a rabbi on practical details.

question: Quelle prière pour une femme le matin
expected:
- Les femmes sont exemptées des mitsvot positives liées au temps (Chema, tefilin), mais selon la Michna/Guemara (Berakhot 20b) elles sont obligées dans la tefila, car c'est une demande de miséricorde.
- Machloket sur l'étendue de l'obligation : selon le Rambam (suivi par le Maguen Avraham), une prière quotidienne de supplication suffit, avec louange, demande et remerciement, même en ses propres mots, par exemple après Modé Ani ou les bénédictions du matin ; selon le Ramban (et la Michna Beroura), elles sont obligées dans la Amida de Cha'harit (et de Min'ha) comme les hommes.
- Il faut au minimum citer les bénédictions du matin (Birkot Hacha'har), dont « ché'assani kirtsono » à la place de « ché'assani isha / 'eved », ainsi que les Birkot HaTorah, que les femmes récitent selon le Choul'han Aroukh.
- Le Chema : les femmes en sont exemptées, mais il est recommandé de dire au moins le premier verset (Chéma Israël) pour accepter le joug du Royaume des Cieux (Choul'han Aroukh 70:1, Rama).
- Un programme minimal recommandé : Modé Ani, Birkot Hacha'har, Birkot HaTorah, Chéma (au moins le premier verset), et si possible la Amida. Si elle en a le temps, elle peut aussi dire les Pessouké Dezimra, Baroukh Chéamar et Ichtaba'h, selon les différentes opinions.
- Il faut tenir compte des circonstances, comme une mère de jeunes enfants : de nombreux décisionnaires autorisent alors à se limiter à une courte prière ou aux bénédictions du matin.

question: Who holds to take off the tefillin during hallel
expected:
- The question mainly concerns Chol HaMoed, not Rosh Chodesh. On Rosh Chodesh the standard ruling (Shulchan Arukh OC 423:4) is to remove tefillin before Musaf, not before or during Hallel. In practice this is usually after Kedusha of Uva Letziyon / before Musaf.
- On Chol HaMoed, wearing tefillin is itself disputed. Shulchan Arukh (following the Zohar and Kabbalah) rules not to wear them, as do Sephardim, Chassidim, the Gra's followers and most of Eretz Yisrael. Many Ashkenazim in the Diaspora follow the Rema and do wear them.
- Among Ashkenazim who wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed, the widespread custom, cited by the Rema and the Acharonim (Mishna Berura), is to remove them before Hallel. Hallel and Musaf have a festival character, and tefillin are an 'ot', which clashes with the day's own 'ot'.
- Other communities wearing tefillin on Chol HaMoed wait until after Hallel, or until before Musaf. The answer should present these as local minhagim.
- Removing tefillin literally in the middle of Hallel is not a recognized practice, since one should not interrupt Hallel. The timing is before Hallel or after it.
- Practice follows one's community or shul minhag; ask a rabbi when unsure.

question: Of the approximately 50 kinot recited on Tisha B'Av, how many (and identify them by the number and first line) directly or implicitly reference the destruction of the Temple (beit HaMikdash). Do not provide any background or context, just the list of kinot and how they reference the Temple.
expected:
- Format: gives what was asked — a list of kinot by number and first line, each with a brief note on how it references the Temple (direct or implicit) — with no extended background. At most it briefly names the edition or rite whose numbering it follows.
- Numbering: the count and numbering differ by edition and rite (e.g., the Ashkenazi Goldschmidt, Rosenfeld or Artscroll/Koren kinot; the Sephardi kinot are a different corpus). A good answer states which edition it follows, or flags that numbers vary.
- Overall count: virtually all of the kinot reference the Churban directly or implicitly. This includes kinot whose main subject is something else, such as the death of Yoshiyahu, the Ten Martyrs, the Crusade massacres, or the burning of the Talmud. Those kinot are framed through, compared with, or juxtaposed to the destruction of the Mikdash.
- Clearly direct examples are correctly identified, such as: 'Lamah le-netzach zanachta' and other kinot built on alphabetic acrostics and verses from Eichah; 'Im tochalnah nashim piryam' (Doeg's son, Zechariah the priest's blood in the Temple); 'Zechor asher asah tzar' (Titus in the Holy of Holies); 'Az be-halokh Yirmiyahu al kivrei avot'; the Zionides ('Tziyon halo tish'ali' and its imitations); 'Eli Tziyon ve-areha'.
- Implicit cases are explained accurately: 'Arzei ha-Levanon' (Ten Martyrs); Kalonymus's kinah on the Crusades, which equates those massacres with the Churban and therefore puts them on Tisha B'Av rather than a new fast day; 'Sha'ali serufah ba-esh' (Maharam of Rothenburg, burning of the Talmud), which draws Temple and Sinai imagery; 'Esh tukad be-kirbi' (contrasting the Exodus with the destruction).
- Honesty: if the answer cannot reliably reconstruct the full numbered list, it says so rather than fabricating numbers or first lines.

question: List sources for the subject of Shmonei Esrei repetition, in particular mind to compose a kuntres giving chizuk for this area called "The Terrifying Chazaras Hashas Guide"
expected:
- Gives the Talmudic basis: the chazzan repeats the Amidah to discharge those who cannot pray themselves (Rosh Hashanah 34b–35a, machloket Rabban Gamliel and Chachamim), and the Rishonim's explanation that the repetition stays an institution even when everyone knows how to daven.
- Cites the core halachic sources: Tur and Shulchan Arukh OC 124 with Mishnah Berurah. These cover listening, the need for nine attentive men, answering Amen and Baruch Hu u'Varuch Shemo, and especially 124:7: one who talks during chazarat hashatz is a sinner whose sin is too great to bear, and he is rebuked.
- Includes sources on the gravity and reward of answering Amen, e.g. Shabbat 119b (whoever answers Amen with all his strength) and Berakhot 47a (not answering a truncated or 'orphaned' Amen). Also notes the Shulchan Arukh's guidance to stand, attend, and not learn during the repetition.
- Mentions the historical and chizuk material behind talking-in-shul warnings, such as the Tosafot Yom Tov's Mi Sheberach for those who refrain from talking during davening (after the 1648 massacres) and later mussar literature. Any such attribution must be accurate or clearly flagged.
- Notes that practice varies: the Rambam abolished the silent Amidah in favor of a single public recitation in Egypt (Teshuvot HaRambam), which was later reversed. - Organizes the sources usefully for a kuntres (e.g., by theme: basis, obligations, the sin of talking, the reward of Amen), possibly with a short suggestion to balance the 'terrifying' tone with positive motivation.

question: I question whether a person can pray for the thoughts or equation of their children of evil thoughts, as everybody is responsible for their own good or bad deeds. Here we see Job praying for his children's thoughts.
expected:
- Job 1:5 describes Job rising early and offering burnt offerings for each of his children after their feasts, out of concern that they may have sinned and 'blessed' (a euphemism for cursed) God in their hearts. Chazal link the olah to atonement for sinful thoughts (hirhur ha-lev). Job is acting both as a concerned father and on their behalf.
- Free will is real: 'Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven' (Berakhot 33b). Each person is ultimately accountable for their own choices, so prayer cannot force another person to be righteous or replace their own teshuvah.
- Praying for another person's spiritual welfare is nonetheless well established in Tanakh and Chazal. David prays that Solomon be given a whole heart (I Chronicles 29:19). Moshe prays that Yehoshua be saved from the spies' counsel (Sotah 34b). Beruriah teaches that one should pray for sins, not sinners, to cease (Berakhot 10a). Our daily liturgy asks for help for ourselves and others: 've-ten be-libenu', 've-yachel levavenu', 'hashiveinu'.
- The resolution: prayer does not override free will. It can bring heavenly assistance, a better environment, good influences, clarity and protection from tests, and opportunities for teshuvah. The choice itself still remains the child's.
- Parents carry a real responsibility for their children's education and spiritual direction, so praying for them, especially for their yirat shamayim, is a recognized and praised practice. Examples include the custom of praying for children to be Torah scholars, associated with Shabbat candle lighting, and the blessing of children.
- A balanced answer acknowledges the tension the questioner raises rather than dismissing it. It explains that personal accountability and intercessory prayer coexist.

question: What is the Amidah prayer?

- Origin: it began as a closing doxology after Torah study/aggadic discourse in the Talmudic period and became part of the liturgy. Its Aramaic is often explained as the vernacular of the time.

question: Dis-moi, dans le passage de Moshé qui fait paître les brebis, il y a ces deux expressions ; y a-t-il un rapport avec les 22 lettres de l'alphabet ? אֶת-צֹאן et אֶת-הַצֹּאן
expected:
- Identifier le verset : Exode (Chemot) 3:1, « וּמֹשֶׁה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת-צֹאן יִתְרוֹ חֹתְנוֹ... וַיִּנְהַג אֶת-הַצֹּאן אַחַר הַמִּדְבָּר ».
